title: A multi‐scale spatial framework for simulating land use carbon risks and ecological compensation under future development scenarios
content:
Abstract

Land-use change creates spatial mismatches between carbon emissions, coefficient-based potential carbon uptake, and ecological compensation responsibilities. Using land-use, energy-consumption, and socioeconomic data from 2000 to 2024, this study develops a Prediction–Assessment–Zoning framework for the Yellow River Basin (YRB), China. The framework integrates land-use carbon accounting, a Carbon Emission and Absorption Coupling Risk (CEACR) index, bivariate LISA, PLUS-based land-use simulation, GM-LSTM-based energy-emission prediction, and K-means clustering for carbon compensation zoning. The estimated uptake in this study refers to coefficient-based potential carbon uptake rather than observed net ecosystem productivity. The results show that the mean CEACR value increased from 0.0193 in 2000 to 0.0279 in 2024, representing a 44.56% increase, while the proportion of extremely high-risk areas rose from 1.92% to 2.79%. High-risk clusters expanded mainly in urban-industrial areas of the middle and lower reaches, indicating clear cross-boundary spillover of land-use carbon risk. Under the 2030 urban development scenario, the mean CEACR value reached 0.0347, 22.6% higher than that under the natural development scenario, whereas low-carbon development and cropland protection constrained risk growth. The low-carbon scenario reduced total land-use carbon emissions by 15.05% compared with the natural development scenario. Based on ECC, ESC, and spatial risk patterns, Shandong, Henan, and Ningxia were identified as payment zones; Qinghai, Sichuan, and Inner Mongolia as compensation zones; and Shanxi, Shaanxi, and Gansu as balanced zones.
